title: Ray Dalio: Advice for the Next Generation (AI Era).
synopsis: An interview clip: Ray Dalio on what he'd tell a 16-year-old about careers in the AI era, widening into debt cycles, inequality and the UK.
claim: Naming a target job is the wrong advice in a period of rapid change, because what compounds is knowing your own nature, maximising your ability to learn (AI included), and staying adaptable enough to move as the paths shift.
points: His refusal to name a job is the substance, not a dodge: he says naming one would mislead them, since "learn to code" was the safe answer right up until agentic coding tools arrived, and the next shift is equally unforeseeable.
Adaptability over intelligence or effort - his framing is that the species and people who succeed are the most adaptable, not the brightest or the hardest working.

Match the work to your nature, but do not ignore the money. Get above the level where you would have to panic, which he ties to how many months you could live without income, and then optimise for work you would want anyway. He points to his free online personality assessment as the entry point for the self-knowledge half.

On inequality he argues a floor - education, adequate housing, healthcare - is in society's own interest, illustrated with Connecticut's high-school dropout and incarceration figures, and that redistribution funding consumption rather than productivity makes the problem worse.

On wealth taxes he is mechanically sceptical (assets must be sold to pay them, which can burst bubbles) and prefers reforms like stepped-up basis. On the UK he is blunt - over-indebted, under-productive, out of choices - and would tell a young founder to be global rather than provincial, citing the expression that a smart rabbit has three holes.
reasoning: , and the two halves deserve different weight. The career advice is honest, and refusing to name a job is more useful than the confident predictions this genre usually produces - but it is also the most generic possible form of the answer. The macro half is Dalio's long-standing debt-cycle thesis delivered as diagnosis rather than argument, and the UK claim in particular is a strong assertion with no counter-case offered; treat it as one prominent investor's read, not a forecast, and note that he is pointing at his own framework and assessment tool throughout. The available transcript cuts off mid-answer, so the closing section is not covered here.
selling: His free Principles U personality assessment, named twice. Nothing is priced, but the interview functions throughout as promotion for his Principles framework and books.

- If the self-knowledge half interests you, the Principles U assessment is free and takes about 30 minutes - worth an evening, and no more than that.
watch: No. It is two people in chairs; nothing visual carries any part of the argument.
